cards.we: strive for excellence in all we do
so: excellence becomes both a habit and an expectation, with all students and staff supported to achieve the highest standards regardless of background or starting point.

cards.we: strive for unity in all we do
so: every student and staff member benefits from a shared mission, collective belief and a consistent world-class education.

cards.we: strive for a no excuses culture in all we do
so: barriers to learning are not accepted but addressed, enabling every student and staff member to achieve their full potential.

cards.we: never stand still and are always improving
so: students and staff continually reflect, learn and grow, striving to be better than before.

cards.we: don’t accept ‘good enough’ and try our best – no excuses
so: students and staff hold high expectations of themselves and take responsibility for their effort and outcomes.

cards.we: bring out the best in each other
so: students and staff support, challenge and inspire one another to succeed together.

cards.we: never place limitations on what we can achieve
so: students and staff believe in their potential and pursue ambitious goals with confidence.

cards.we: are defined not by where we come from, but by where we are going
so: students and staff recognise that background does not limit potential and that everyone has the right, responsibility and opportunity to succeed.

cards.we: relentlessly focus on achieving exceptional outcomes
so: students understand that exam results open doors to a world of choices and bright futures, regardless of background or circumstance.
students are not limited in the choices they can make, the quality of life they can achieve, or the impact they can have in their community.

cards.we: believe knowledge is power and pursue academic excellence every day
so: students are unashamed in striving for and achieving the best possible outcomes, thereby expanding their future opportunities.

cards.we: ensure students see themselves as equal to everyone else
so: students understand their worth and never accept being treated—or treating themselves—as less than others.

cards.we: develop students’ confidence and self-belief
so: students recognise their value, stand with dignity, and engage with others as equals in all aspects of school life.

cards.we: encourage curiosity and ambition
so: students actively seek and seize opportunities to excel beyond perceived limits.

cards.we: value and model hard work, reliability and responsibility
so: students develop the habits and attitudes needed to succeed in education, work, and life.

cards.we: normalise challenge and learning from failure
so: students build perseverance and know how to recover, reflect, and move forward with confidence.

cards.we: explicitly teach oracy through agreed structures, language expectations and classroom talk routines
so: students know how to contribute purposefully, articulate ideas and engage in meaningful dialogue.

cards.we: create a culture where challenge, effort and reflection are interwoven in the fabric of school life
so: students develop resilience, learn from setbacks and confidently pick themselves back up when things do not go to plan.

cards.we: model and consistently reinforce the Mossbourne values of Excellence, Unity and No Excuses across all aspects of school life
so: students develop pride in representing themselves and the Mossbourne community positively.

cards.we: create a strong sense of belonging and collective identity
so: students feel proud to be Mossbournians and recognise that their actions reflect both themselves and others.

cards.we: are unapologetically ambitious for every student’s academic achievement, recognising that strong educational outcomes are closely linked to greater life chances, long-term wellbeing and social mobility (Department for Education; Social Mobility Commission; Public Health England)
so: students gain the qualifications, knowledge and cultural capital associated with greater access to higher education, sustained employment and higher lifetime earnings.
students are better protected against the long-term effects of disadvantage, recognising that education is one of the most significant drivers of social mobility and opportunity in adulthood.

students develop the literacy, confidence and critical thinking skills linked to positive adult wellbeing, independence and participation in society (Public Health England, Health Profile for England).
every young person leaves school with the academic foundations associated with healthier life outcomes, increased agency and wider opportunities across adult life.

cards.we: set aspirational targets for all our students based on their starting points
so: students are aware of our belief in them and strive for the very highest grades possible.

cards.we: map core knowledge on knowledge organisers (KOs) and test students on it regularly
so: foundational knowledge needed to access the curriculum is secured.
cognitive load is decreased to allow students to learn and remember new knowledge.
knowledge-webs (or schema) develop in complexity as new knowledge ‘sticks’ to existing knowledge.

cards.we: retest students who underperform in KO tests
so: we do not give up on the student and show we believe they can do it.
we do not allow knowledge gaps to persist or grow.
we develop students’ resilience and growth mindset.

cards.we: formally test students on what they have learned three times per year
so: success and effort are formally recognised and celebrated.
resilience and revision skills are developed proportionately.
students, teachers, and parents have a clear understanding of progress and any concerns.
we can intervene meaningfully and with impact if support is required.

cards.we: test reading ability at least once a year
so: we can help all students to read at least in line with their chronological age.

cards.we: stream students in Years 7 and Year 8
so: lesson pace and pitch can be optimised while the curriculum content remains the same and as ambitious for all learners.

cards.we: set students in Years 9, Year 10 and Year 11
so: subject groupings can be more closely tailored to students as content becomes more complex and specialised.
lesson pace and pitch can be optimised while the curriculum content remains the same and as ambitious for all learners.

cards.we: review streams (Year 7 and 8) and sets (Year 9, 10 and 11) in light of assessment data and teacher feedback where appropriate, with Year 7 reviewed in the Autumn term and all other year groups in the spring term and at the end of the school year
so: groupings remain appropriate for all learners, allowing initial KS2 and SATs data anomalies to be identified and addressed in Year 7.
all students benefit from a shared curriculum and expert teaching regardless of teaching group.
disruption to students is minimised by avoiding changes to teaching groups where subjects are timetabled in blocks, as one change can lead to multiple new teachers.

cards.we: have a three-year Key Stage 3 curriculum
so: choice and breadth is retained for as long as possible.

cards.we: “bake-in” the knowledge and skills needed for long-term wellbeing and success into our curriculum design
so: opportunities for personal growth are experienced by every student, not only those who seek them out independently.
the curriculum reflects the qualities and values we want students to carry into adulthood.
the curriculum intentionally develops the character, habits and competencies that enable long-term success and wellbeing.

cards.we: prioritise subject disciplines that help students explore culture, history, creativity and what it means to be human
so: students develop empathy, cultural understanding and a deeper awareness of the world and their place within it.
students understand the beliefs, histories and ideas that have shaped societies and continue to influence how people think and live today.
students learn to think critically, reflect thoughtfully and engage meaningfully with the complexities of human experience.
students reflect on humanity’s past, present and future, developing a deeper understanding of themselves and the world around them.
students develop the distinctly human qualities — such as empathy, reflection, creativity and critical thought — that will remain vital in a changing modern world.

cards.we: use bespoke precision curriculum booklets, designed and regularly reviewed and improved by expert teachers, and require all students to use them regardless of set
so: all students access a carefully sequenced, high-quality curriculum that secures core knowledge and reduces variability in provision.
we can ensure that key learning points are delivered to every student we teach.
expectations remain consistently high for all learners, supporting equity and ensuring no student is disadvantaged by grouping.
teachers can deliver with clarity and precision, enabling students to consolidate learning and prevent gaps from developing.
revision resources are centralised in one place, supporting independent study and minimising gaps in knowledge, including those caused by absence.

teacher time is freed to focus on responsive teaching, engaging with students’ work and delivering content effectively to meet the needs of their classes, particularly the most able and those who need additional support.

cards.we: give Year 9 students a choice of ‘Creative Electives’, such as music, drama, art, food science or technology, to study for half a year
so: students can choose their preferred creative subjects without limiting their access to creativity and the arts.
students develop their understanding of the subject ahead of choosing their GCSE options.

cards.we: give KS3 students in the lowest attaining groups an extra hour of maths and English
so: students are supported in catching up with their peers and closing knowledge gaps before GCSE.

cards.we: ensure all students have the opportunity to learn a modern foreign language from Year 7 until the end of Year 11
so: students develop the linguistic knowledge, cultural understanding and communication skills needed to thrive in an increasingly interconnected world.
students benefit from a broad, ambitious curriculum that is comparable in scope and aspiration to that offered in the private sector.
students acquire lasting knowledge and qualifications that open doors to further study, employment and future opportunities.

cards.we: provide key groups of students with the opportunity to study an extra language, such as Latin, Turkish etc, subject to timetabling and staffing capacity
so: students are stretched, challenged and have the same curriculum opportunities as students in selective or fee-paying schools.
enrichment and equity are balanced, enabling some students to access additional languages while ensuring others focus on securing fundamental knowledge and skills.
students who have English as an Additional Language (EAL) are able to celebrate and improve their knowledge of their mother tongue.

cards.we: expect students to participate in the full curriculum offer
so: students are not disadvantaged at a later stage of their education.
students have the experience of feeling difficulty and persevering, learning resilience and their own strength.
students are treated with parity.
public funds are spent responsibly and not wasted.

cards.we: require all students to study History and Religious Studies at GCSE
so: students develop cultural and historical understanding and moral perspective.
students’ spiritual, moral, social and cultural (SMSC) development is strengthened, enabling them to reflect on beliefs, values, identity and ethical issues in a diverse society.
students are not forced to choose between History and Geography.
students read and write at length across the curriculum, developing their reading and writing ability which is correlated with future wellbeing and opportunities.
students develop as independent, critical thinkers, able to analyse evidence, evaluate different perspectives and construct well reasoned judgements.

cards.we: require all students to study the English Baccalaureate suite of subjects (English, Maths, at least 2 sciences, a humanities subject and a foreign language)
so: all students study a broad and ambitious curriculum, building strong academic foundations across disciplines.
we are raising rather than lowering the academic floor for our students to safeguard their future opportunities.
disadvantaged students have access to the same academic opportunities as the most advantaged.
all students have access to a diverse range of modes of academic thought: analytical problem-solving, the analysis and usage of language and an appreciation of the past and other cultures.

cards.we: offer one KS4 option rather than two
so: space is created on student timetables for co-curricular provision that supports student wellbeing at a time of exam stress (e.g. through the Bourne Scholar and Prep programme, as well as core PE)
students develop a love of learning for its own sake, valuing knowledge and curiosity beyond assessment outcomes or certification.
students must continue to be creative and active via the Bourne Scholar programme, building life-long habits associated with increased wellbeing.
students leave with at least 9 GCSEs (some with more), in line with the most successful schools.

cards.we: deliberately map, embed, and monitor our personal development offer intentionally across the taught curriculum and the wider co curricular offer
so: personal growth is shaped consistently over time for all students and not left to chance.

cards.we: hold fortnightly whole-school assemblies
so: students develop a shared sense of identity, values and purpose, strengthening culture and belonging.
key messages around behaviour, expectations, safeguarding and aspiration are consistently reinforced so that standards remain high and understood by all.
structured opportunities to celebrate success and model excellence are created, ensuring all students are exposed to the same high expectations.

cards.we: provide daily tutor time for all students
so: students are consistently supported by a familiar trusted adult in developing routines, organisation and a strong sense of belonging within the school community.
key messages around attendance, behaviour, safeguarding and personal development are reinforced daily, ensuring clarity and consistency of expectations.
concerns and targeted support can be identified early, helping to prevent gaps in learning, wellbeing or engagement from developing.

cards.we: have at least three drop-down days a year dedicated to Personal Development
so: students have a high-quality, bespoke programme delivered by specialists.

cards.we: timetable a weekly Bourne Scholar lesson dedicated to a wide-range of co-curricular subjects, such as Ancient Worlds; Local History; Charity & Advocacy; Storytelling; First Aid; Philosophy; Yoga & Mindfulness etc.
so: students encounter ideas and disciplines beyond the curriculum.
disadvantaged students have access to powerful knowledge in line with the most advantaged in our society.
students have a dedicated space to discuss and debate ideas in the curriculum.

cards.we: formalise co-curricular opportunities via Prep (e.g. Big Debates, School Production, Jack Petchey Speak Out competition, Prep Club Programme, Burning Question); Friday afternoons (e.g. Combined Cadet Force; Duke of Edinburgh; trip programme; primary school volunteering); Saturdays (e.g. Co-curricular Saturdays or Saturday Schools), and break/lunch times and after/ before school (e.g. sports clubs and fixtures; music ensembles and choirs; Learning Area Enrichment Weeks; Culture Week)
so: co-curricular access is not a luxury for a few, but an entitlement for all.
all students can develop a hobby or interest beyond the curriculum.
all students given the opportunity to step outside their comfort zone and experience something new.

cards.we: prioritise Religious Studies and History on the KS3 and KS4 curriculum
so: students develop a robust awareness and understanding of the events, ideas and beliefs that have shaped our world.
students develop as independent, critical thinkers, able to analyse evidence, evaluate different perspectives and construct well reasoned judgements.
students’ spiritual, moral, social and cultural (SMSC) development is strengthened, enabling them to reflect on beliefs, values, identity and ethical issues in a diverse society.
students understand the importance of standing up to injustice and intolerance when they witness it.
students read and write at length across the curriculum, developing their reading and writing ability which is correlated with future wellbeing and opportunities.

cards.we: provide Preparation (Prep) as part of students’ timetables where they can complete independent study, homework and self-quizzing from Knowledge Organisers
so: students are supported in consolidating knowledge and developing habits and study skills that will support them in the future.

barriers linked to inequality, including limited space, resources or support at home, are reduced, ensuring all students have equitable access to purposeful independent study and preventing gaps in learning from developing.

cards.we: reduce the amount of Prep for students as they progress through the school and/or demonstrate the ability to work independently, meet deadlines and produce work of a consistently high standard
so: students progressively develop independence, with scaffolding reduced over time as they build effective study habits, resilience, and responsibility for their own learning.

students are recognised for independence and consistency through Prep Privilege, where eligible students may be released earlier when demonstrating high standards of work completion, behaviour and academic responsibility, recognising that students develop at different rates and require varying levels of support.

cards.we: provide opportunities for student leadership and responsibility, such as Student Council or Parliament, Ambassadors, Student Helpers with younger year groups, CCF etc.
so: students have opportunities to develop their confidence in finding their voice, making decisions, being a positive role model and leading others.

cards.we: celebrate collective as well as individual success, such as year group attendance, punctuality, co-curricular success and achievement marks
so: students understand the value of contributing to something larger than themselves.

cards.we: celebrate student success frequently, deliberately and publicly, for example via achievement marks, subject awards, pastoral awards, celebration assemblies, shout-outs and recognition displays
so: positive behaviour, effort and character are consistently recognised and reinforced across the school.
students understand that success is noticed, valued, and shared, helping to build pride in achievement and a strong sense of belonging.
we create a culture where excellence, kindness and consistency are visible and aspirational for all students.

students are motivated not only by meeting expectations, but by striving to contribute positively to the wider school community and to be recognised for the habits that will support them in future academic and professional life.

cards.we: explicitly support staff in developing positive relationships with students through our professional development programme and shared pedagogical rubric
so: positive relationships are systematically developed and sustained, supporting a calm, inclusive and effective learning environment.

cards.we: expect students to show courtesy, respect, and politeness to all members of the academy community and visitors
so: a culture of respect is established, and all members of the community feel safe, valued, and supported.
students develop strong interpersonal skills and social awareness that prepare them for the adults they will become.

cards.we: say a shared school reflection before every lesson: Throughout this lesson I aspire to maintain an enquiring mind, a calm disposition, and an attentive ear, so that in this class, and all classes, I can fulfil my true potential
so: unity and a shared sense of identity as a proud member of the Mossbourne community is promoted amongst staff and students.
students are consistently reminded of the habits and attitudes that lead to success, creating focus and readiness for learning.
a calm, purposeful start to every lesson is established, reducing transition time, and improving engagement from the outset.
key values are embedded through repetition, helping students internalise behaviours that support both academic success and personal development.
consistency across all classrooms ensures fairness and predictability for all students.

cards.we: line up students in the playground at key transition points during the school day
so: all students can be quickly and accurately accounted for at key points in the day.
students experience a calm and prompt start to lessons, helping them to be settled, focused and set up for success.
staff can carry out essential checks, including uniform, equipment and planner expectations and support where needed.
movement around the school is orderly, calm and safe, reducing congestion and risk.
any immediate concerns relating to attendance, punctuality or student wellbeing can be identified and followed up.
students are consistently prepared and ready to learn, supporting strong routines and high expectations across the school.

cards.we: ‘sweat the small stuff’ by addressing minor behaviours consistently and early
so: serious behaviour that impacts all students’ right to a calm, safe and focused learning environment is less likely to occur.
clear boundaries are established so that expectations remain predictable and secure for everyone.

students internalise high standards and self-discipline, preparing them to see themselves as the professionals of tomorrow—whether in medicine, law, engineering, or any field of their choosing where precision, conduct and responsibility define success.

cards.we: apply behaviour expectations and sanctions consistently across all classrooms and staff
so: students experience clear, predictable expectations that help them understand how to succeed.
a shared sense of fairness and justice is maintained, where all students are treated equitably.
uncertainty is reduced, supporting all learners—and particularly those with SEND or additional needs—who benefit from structure and consistency.
students experience a calm, safe and emotionally predictable environment, recognising that consistency and routine are particularly important for those who may have experienced trauma or instability.

cards.we: respond to behaviour in a uniform and non-negotiable way
so: students are not required to interpret different expectations between teachers or contexts.
attention is focused on learning rather than navigating inconsistency.
students develop confidence in the systems around them and trust in adults.

cards.we: challenge and sanction any disruption consistently, recognising that every moment of disruption affects students’ right to learn
so: learning time is protected for all students, not just those causing disruption.
students understand that there is no acceptable level of disruption when it impacts others.
a culture of focus, respect and self-regulation is established across all classrooms.

cards.we: use volume and tone intentionally and proportionately, including a raised or sharp volume and/or tone when appropriate, in line with DfE guidance
so: students learn to recognise the urgency or severity of a situation, respect adult authority, and benefit from a structured environment that supports their wellbeing and success.
expectations are clear, students are protected, and adults can maintain calm, purposeful learning environments in the best interests of students.
students experience school as a safe and predictable environment where dignity is protected, and positive relationships underpin learning and behaviour.

cards.we: maintain clear adult authority in our interactions with students, using tone, volume, presence and boundaries as necessary and appropriately
so: students feel secure in adults being the decision-makers and are not placed under pressure to manage situations beyond their developmental readiness.
ambiguity is reduced, preventing anxiety, confusion or inconsistency, and students experience clarity that supports success.

cards.we: avoid approaches that transfer adult responsibility to students, such as allowing negotiation of boundaries or sanctions, and instead assert calm, consistent adult authority
so: students are supported to thrive within clear, predictable and secure structures, rather than being expected to manage excessive autonomy before they are ready.
clear boundaries create a sense of safety and consistency, reducing anxiety and enabling students to focus on learning and growth.
students are explicitly taught how and when to respond appropriately, enabling independence to develop gradually and successfully.
strong, positive relationships can flourish, including appropriate warmth, humour and informality, because everyone understands where the boundaries sit.
students learn how to have their voice heard respectfully, navigate relationships confidently, and prepare for future environments such as university and the workplace.

cards.we: ask students involved in serious behaviour incidents to write a factual account of what happened
so: their voice is heard, emotional regulation is supported, and adults can respond fairly, consistently and in students’ best interests.

cards.we: use the school planner as the primary tool for communication with parents regarding both achievements and sanctions
so: parents can engage directly with their child’s day-to-day school experience, celebrating successes such as achievement marks and recognising areas for improvement, including detentions where issued.
parents are supported in having timely, informed conversations with their child, reinforcing positive behaviour, and helping to correct patterns of conduct at home as well as in school.
engagement with homework, prep and independent study is strengthened, as parents can clearly see what has been set and support their child in developing consistent study habits.
parents and students maintain a clear, tangible record of achievements, sanctions and communication over time.
the system remains fully inclusive and equitable, ensuring all students and families have equal access to communication regardless of access to technology or digital devices.
students develop organisation, accountability and the habit of sharing important information appropriately and consistently with home.

students are supported in developing organisation and responsibility for their learning resources, particularly in the absence of universal access to lockers, by enabling clear daily planning for equipment and preparation for the school day ahead.

cards.we: expect students to be focused, attentive and fully engaged in lessons
so: learning time is maximised and disruption is minimised.
students develop resilience, concentration and the habits required for academic and personal success.
achievement builds confidence and fosters a lasting love of learning.

cards.we: require students to follow instructions from staff without argument and address concerns appropriately
so: learning time is protected and not diverted by prolonged discussions, ensuring all students remain focused and ready to learn.
students develop patience, self-regulation and the ability to respond calmly and respectfully, even when they disagree.
students learn that not every concern can or should be resolved immediately, and that reflection and appropriate timing are important life skills.
students are prepared for professional environments where following instructions, managing emotions and addressing issues appropriately are essential to success.
the school environment remains orderly and predictable, supporting all learners.

cards.we: treat defiance in tone, including sarcasm, disrespectful responses, or undermining language, as a serious behaviour issue
so: clear boundaries are maintained around respectful communication between students and staff.
learning time is protected and not disrupted by prolonged challenge or escalation in dialogue.
students develop appropriate ways of expressing disagreement or difficulty that reflect maturity and readiness for future professional environments.
a calm, respectful and orderly school culture is maintained where all members of the community feel valued and safe.

cards.we: take all forms of bullying, discriminatory behaviour, and prejudice-related incidents extremely seriously
so: every student feels safe, included, and respected within the school community.
clear and consistent boundaries are maintained so that harmful behaviour is challenged immediately and appropriately.
students understand the impact of their words and actions on others, and are supported to develop empathy, respect, and responsibility.
we uphold a culture where difference is valued and protected, and where all students can learn and thrive without fear of intimidation or exclusion.

cards.we: treat chewing gum, littering and damage to school property as serious issues
so: students take pride in their environment and understand their role in maintaining shared spaces.
the school remains clean, safe and respectful for all members of the community.
resources are preserved for teaching and learning and co-curricular opportunities rather than being redirected to address avoidable damage.
students develop habits of care and responsibility that extend beyond school.

cards.we: do not allow students to eat outside out of designated eating zones
so: we discourage students from littering, ensuring a pleasant environment free from pests.
students are encouraged to develop healthy routines around eating, including structured mealtimes with friends that support healthy lifestyles and wellbeing.

cards.we: do not allow students to bring in fizzy or caffeinated drinks
so: students are encouraged to develop healthy habits, avoiding sugary or caffeinated beverages.
the risk of damage because of spills and stains is reduced.
students develop the habit of using refillable water bottles, helping to reduce costs for families and encourage environmentally responsible choices.

cards.we: require students to ask staff permission to move beyond their seat, drink water or take off their blazer
so: learning is not disrupted by constant and unnecessary movement.
expectations are consistent across classrooms to support students.
teachers maintain clear authority and professional control of the classroom.
students remain focused, calm, and fully engaged in their learning.

cards.we: require all students to bring the full set of essential equipment (including a minimum of two black pens, two green pens, pencils, highlighters, glue stick, headphones, pencil case, dictionary, mathematical protractor, set square, ruler, eraser, scientific calculator, reading book, colouring pencils and subject-specific items) and address missing equipment promptly and consistently
so: lessons begin without disruption and learning time is maximised.
students develop organisation, independence, and responsibility in preparation for adult life.
minor lapses are addressed early to maintain high standards and prevent escalation.
all students are equipped equally, supporting fairness, engagement, and readiness to learn.

cards.we: expect students to go directly home after school and not congregate in groups or detour into shops or other locations in school uniform
so: students are safeguarded by reducing exposure to risks in public spaces, including potential incidents of theft, conflict, or exploitation.
parents know where their child is expected to be at the end of the school day, supporting clear responsibility, oversight, and wellbeing.
students develop routines of responsibility and time management by moving safely and efficiently between school and home.
we minimise opportunities for students to become involved in or witness incidents of poor behaviour in the community.

cards.we: do not allow students to carry money
so: students are less vulnerable to theft or peer pressure in school or the local area.
we reduce safeguarding risks linked to carrying valuables on the journey to and from school.
opportunities for poor behaviour linked to carrying money or valuables are reduced, helping students make safe and responsible choices throughout the school day.

cards.we: deploy staff on duty in the local community after school
so: students have visible, trusted adults available should they need support, reassurance, or intervention on their journey home.
links between school and community are strengthened, reinforcing a shared responsibility for student safety and wellbeing.

cards.we: do not allow physical contact between students in school or on the way to/from school
so: clear, unambiguous boundaries protect all students from unwanted or misinterpreted touch and ensure personal space is consistently respected.
we eliminate grey areas where behaviour could be misunderstood or overlooked.
we minimise the risk of misunderstandings or misinterpretations between students escalating into conflict or confrontation.
all students feel safe, secure, and confident that their personal boundaries will be upheld at all times.
we support students in developing respectful social behaviour that prepares them for appropriate conduct in wider society and future workplaces.

cards.we: keep playground groups to a prescribed number
so: staff can maintain clear visibility and supervision, ensuring safeguarding is effective and proactive.
potential for conflict, exclusion or bullying behaviour is reduced through structured social organisation.
students are more able to participate in conversation, supporting oracy development and ensuring that all voices are heard within smaller, more structured social groups.

cards.we: require silent and orderly movement in inside corridors between lessons
so: students move calmly and safely through the school environment, reducing opportunities for disruption or unobserved poor behaviour.
expectations are applied consistently and fairly, ensuring all students experience the same calm and structured transitions.
students, particularly those with SEND, are supported through predictable, low-stimulation movement between lessons.
we create a calm and purposeful atmosphere across the school that reflects high standards of behaviour at all times of the day.

cards.we: expect students to remain in lessons and only use the toilet at permitted times, except in genuine need, with staff discretion applied at all times
so: students remain appropriately supervised at all times, avoiding unsupervised spaces.
learning time is protected and disruption to lessons is minimised.
students develop self-regulation and responsibility.

cards.we: expect students to remain in lessons and only use the toilet at permitted times, except in genuine need, with staff discretion applied at all times
so: students remain appropriately supervised at all times, avoiding unsupervised spaces.
learning time is protected and disruption to lessons is minimised.
students develop self-regulation and responsibility.

cards.we: require students who leave a lesson to use the toilet to make up lost learning time at break, lunch or after school (including those with toilet passes, where staff professional judgement indicates learning time has been significantly missed)
so: lost learning time is not normalised, and students remain fully engaged with curriculum content.
equitable access to learning time is protected, ensuring gaps in understanding are not created or widened and are addressed through consistent expectations for catch-up.
students recognise that lesson time is essential to securing core knowledge and that missed learning must be recovered to prevent widening gaps and ensure fairness in outcomes.
reasonable adjustments are made in line with medical or welfare requirements, whilst still ensuring equitable access to learning and preventing the development of avoidable learning gaps.

cards.we: require GP medical evidence to support the issuing or continuation of a toilet pass where a long-term or regular need is identified
so: adjustments are based on verified medical need, ensuring consistency, fairness, and appropriate safeguarding.
disruption to learning is minimised and avoidable gaps in learning are prevented.

cards.we: monitor patterns of toilet use during lessons through recording time of toilet use during lessons in the planner and follow up concerns with pastoral teams and parents/carers where appropriate
so: potential welfare or safeguarding concerns can be identified early.
students who may be avoiding learning or experiencing difficulties are supported appropriately.
staff and parents/carers can intervene consistently and sensitively where patterns emerge.

cards.sub: Mobile phones and other communication devices
cards.we: do not allow mobile phones or any other communication device, such as smart watches, iPads, pagers etc. on site, including in bags or on silent
so: students are protected from risks associated with inappropriate use, including online harm, social pressure, or misuse of images.
students are not distracted by notifications, messages, or the temptation to check devices, allowing full focus on learning.
students are fully present in their interactions, supporting wellbeing, confidence, and positive peer relationships.
the learning environment remains calm, purposeful, and free from digital interruption.
students develop habits of sustained attention and self-discipline that are essential for academic success and future employment.
families are not placed in the position of negotiating or managing expectations alone, as the school provides a clear and consistent framework.

cards.sub: Mobile phones and other communication devices
cards.we: extend mobile phone/device expectations to journeys to and from school
so: students are less vulnerable to theft or unwanted attention in the community.
reliance on devices is reduced, encouraging students to engage with their surroundings and make safe, considered decisions, such as when crossing roads or getting on and off public transport.
students develop confidence and independence in navigating real-world situations, including seeking support appropriately from adults when needed.
space is created for genuine interaction and reflection, supporting the development of conversation skills, presence, and overall wellbeing without constant digital distraction.
parents and carers can be confident that students are moving safely and purposefully between school and home.

cards.sub: Mobile phones and other communication devices
cards.we: confiscate mobile phones/ devices for a fixed period including where this period extends into school holidays, in line with national guidance
so: there is a clear, consistent, and meaningful consequence that reinforces our expectations around mobile phone use.
students are supported to break habits of reliance on devices and re-engage fully with learning and face-to-face interaction.
boundaries are applied fairly and predictably for all students, regardless of timing or circumstance.
students experience sustained time without devices, strengthening focus, independence, and self-regulation.
students receive the same message at home and at school, increasing the likelihood of positive habits being established and sustained.

cards.we: use detentions as a response to poor behaviour or unmet expectations
so: students learn that actions have consequences, building accountability and self-discipline.
relationships between students and teachers can be restored through structured reflection and follow-up conversations.
students develop resilience by learning to respond positively to setbacks and correction.

cards.we: use detentions of varying lengths (e.g., 20 minutes, 30 minutes, 1 hour, 2 hours)
so: students experience consequences that are proportionate to the behaviour, reinforcing a clear sense of fairness and justice.
low-level issues are addressed early, preventing them from escalating into more serious concerns.
the opportunity for students to reflect, adjust and improve is built in at every stage.

cards.we: increase the length of detentions where behaviour persists or escalates
so: students understand that repeated poor choices lead to more serious consequences.
patterns of behaviour are disrupted before they become entrenched.
staff can intervene early and effectively, reducing the need for more serious sanctions.

cards.we: communicate our systems for detentions clearly
so: students and families have clarity and predictability around expectations and consequences.

short, routine interventions can be issued immediately, allowing issues to be addressed promptly while also ensuring students have a fresh start the following day without behaviour carrying over unnecessarily.
longer detentions are communicated in advance, allowing families as much time as possible to adjust their plans to support their child, and ensuring fairness and transparency.
we maintain consistency and equity in communication through the planner, ensuring all families receive clear and accessible information about school decisions.

we give parents and carers more notice than stipulated in DfE guidance, which states that advance notice is not required for detentions in most cases, to support parents in knowing their child’s whereabouts.

cards.we: use extended detentions (such as on Saturday mornings) for persistent or serious incidents
so: there is a clear and significant response to behaviour that falls well below expectations.
students and families understand the seriousness of the incident.
a strong opportunity is created for reflection, reset and re-establishing expectations.
we reduce the need for suspensions and permanent exclusions while still upholding high standards.

cards.we: do not exempt students from detentions due to external commitments or seasonal factors like winter darkness
so: expectations remain fair, consistent, and applied equally to all students, regardless of circumstance.
students learn to plan, prioritise, and take responsibility for managing commitments—an essential life skill for adulthood.
we avoid creating variability in consequences, which can undermine a shared sense of justice and clarity across the school.
longer detentions will be communicated in advance so that parents/carers are able to make arrangements for collecting their child if needed.
students develop resilience and adaptability, understanding that commitments and responsibilities often need to be balanced in adult life.

cards.we: issue detentions for unauthorised absence and lateness to school or lessons
so: students understand that punctuality and attendance are fundamental expectations that underpin success in school and beyond.
learning time is protected and curriculum coverage is maintained consistently for all students.
students develop habits of reliability and professionalism that reflect the expectations of future workplaces and careers.
we reduce the impact of social and economic disadvantage by ensuring all students access the full curriculum in real time, rather than relying on catch-up that can widen gaps and affect wellbeing.

cards.we: issue catch-up outside of school hours for extended or repeated absence
so: learning time is protected, knowledge gaps minimised, and curriculum coverage is maintained consistently for all students, regardless of individual circumstances.
high expectations for engagement and progress are upheld consistently, so that absence does not become a barrier to future success or create long-term gaps in understanding.

cards.we: issue detentions for missing or incomplete equipment
so: students develop organisation, independence, and readiness for learning.
learning time is protected and not lost to avoidable disruption.

cards.we: sanction poor-quality or incomplete homework
so: students develop independent study habits essential for future academic and professional success.
learning is consolidated and extended beyond the classroom.
high expectations are maintained consistently for all, reducing gaps between students.

cards.we: remove students from lessons for persistent or serious disruption, or infringements of academy expectations
so: learning is protected for the wider class, ensuring that all students can progress without interruption or loss of teaching time.
students understand that repeated or significant disruption has clear and immediate consequences.

students continue to access the same curriculum content in a supervised setting, using work provided by their classroom teacher, so that learning is not lost but redirected into a more structured environment.
we interrupt patterns of disruption early, preventing longer-term negative impacts on the student’s progress and reducing the likelihood of behavioural escalation.

students are given space to reset, reflect and return to lessons in a more positive and successful frame of mind, rather than remaining in an environment where continued disruption would limit their learning.
we reduce the need for suspensions while still upholding high standards.

cards.we: may, where appropriate, support students by temporarily removing them from lessons or circulation where engagement with core school expectations breaks down
so: we prioritise the long-term best interests of the student by ensuring that communication, expectations and support are realigned in a structured and purposeful way.
there is a clear reset point that re-establishes the importance of partnership between home and school in supporting the student’s progress and wellbeing.
families are reminded of the shared responsibility for a student’s success, reinforcing the home–school agreement as a vital foundation for effective support.

cards.we: may remove students from lessons or circulation for uniform or appearance code breaches
so: school expectations are upheld consistently and visibly, reinforcing that standards apply to all students without exception.
clear boundaries are reinforced across the student body, ensuring that expectations are seen to be meaningful, fair and consistently applied.
we maintain a calm, professional environment where shared standards support a sense of order, pride and belonging.

cards.we: require removed students to continue their work in an alternative space (e.g., outside a Head of Learning Area or Head of Year’s office, or in the Behavioural Support Unit)
so: students remain engaged in the same curriculum as their peers, completing work set by their classroom teacher.
students remain safe, visible and guided by staff at all times.
appropriate support can be given to help students re-engage with their learning.

cards.we: use removal as an opportunity for reflection and reset, for example following a suspension
so: students can regulate their behaviour and complete any missed work, setting them up for a successful reintegration.
time is created for meaningful reflection on actions and their impact.
students begin to rebuild self-control and readiness to learn.

cards.we: require restorative conversations before reintegration into lessons, where needed
so: relationships between students and teachers are repaired and strengthened.
students understand the impact of their behaviour on others and on their own learning.
a clear and positive reset is established before returning to the classroom.

cards.we: expect a parental meeting following removal from a lesson due to persistent or serious behaviour
so: home and school work together to support the student in understanding and changing their behaviour.
there is a shared, consistent message about expectations and consequences across both environments.
students experience a clear reset point, reinforcing the seriousness of the behaviour while also signalling that improvement is expected and supported.
we strengthen the partnership between home and school, ensuring that no child’s behaviour is addressed in isolation from the adults responsible for their development.

cards.we: use suspensions as a serious sanction for significant and/or persistent breaches of behaviour expectations
so: students understand the seriousness of their actions and the impact on the school community.
high standards are maintained consistently, ensuring a safe, calm and orderly learning environment for all.
students are given a structured opportunity to reflect and reset before returning to mainstream learning.

cards.we: support students by ensuring they access existing curriculum resources (such as curriculum booklets, knowledge organisers, homework and prep materials) during shorter suspensions
so: expectations for independent study are supported via resources students already have including knowledge organisers, curriculum booklets, homework, and prep materials, without creating unrealistic administrative burden for staff or families.
staff remain focused on teaching and learning, recognising the significant time required to collate work across multiple subjects within very tight timeframes and busy timetables.

cards.we: provide structured work for longer suspensions
so: students can continue their learning in a meaningful and coordinated way across subjects.
despite the significant administrative time required to gather materials from multiple teachers, continuity of education is maintained.
parents/carers are supported in ensuring students remain engaged with their learning during the exclusion period.

cards.we: expect a formal reintegration meeting involving parents/carers to take place before a student returns to lessons
so: there is a clear shared understanding between home and school of expectations moving forward.
behaviour is addressed in partnership, reinforcing consistency and support across both environments.
students return with clarity and accountability to set them up for future success.

cards.we: do not immediately place students back into mainstream lessons and/or their break periods upon return from a suspension
so: students are supported to transition calmly and successfully back into full lessons.
expectations are reinforced in a structured environment before full reintegration.
staff can ensure readiness for learning while reducing the risk of immediate recurrence of poor behaviour.

cards.we: Objective
so: How our uniform expectations achieve the objective:

cards.we: expect students to adhere to uniform and appearance expectations at all times, including on the journey to and from school and at school events, such as Parents’ Evenings
so: a sense of equality is established, reducing visible differences between students, and supporting social cohesion.
a shared identity and sense of belonging within the school community is strengthened.
opportunities for cliques or negative groups to form are reduced and students’ self-confidence is increased when they do not feel pressured to adopt certain trends.
students’ self-discipline and organisation are developed and becomes habitual, supporting other aspects of education, including behaviour and study skills.
students can focus on learning rather than appearance or comparison, and staff can focus on teaching rather than dealing with potential bullying issues related to appearance.
students are prepared for professional environments where presentation and standards matter.

cards.we: offer two uniform options (Uniform A and Uniform B) rather than prescribing by gender
so: all students can choose a uniform that supports their identity and wellbeing.
inclusion is embedded within a clear and structured system, ensuring all students feel respected and confident.

cards.we: require students to not mix elements of both Uniform A and Uniform B
so: clarity and consistency of expectations are maintained across the school.
the purpose of uniform—equality, simplicity, and professionalism—is preserved.
students are not placed in situations where expectations become unclear or inconsistently applied.

cards.we: apply sanctions for uniform breaches in line with the Behaviour, Attendance, Uniform and Appearance Policy, and children may be sent home, removed from normal circulation or placed in the Behaviour Support Unit
so: expectations are upheld consistently and fairly for all students.
standards remain meaningful, visible and taken seriously across the school community.
students understand that meeting expectations is part of responsibility and self-discipline, setting them up for success at school and beyond.

cards.we: ONLY allow uniform exceptions where required in line with protected characteristics, sincere religious observance and the Equality Act 2010, with final decisions resting with the Principal
so: inclusion and respect for individual needs are upheld.
adjustments are made fairly and appropriately while maintaining consistency for all students.

cards.we: require underclothing, including thermals and vests, to remain unseen.
so: students can meet expectations without pressure to display brands or trends.
consistency and clarity is maintained for all.

cards.we: do not allow trainers outside of PE or the playground
so: students are dressed appropriately for a formal learning environment.
expectations are clear and consistent.
standards prepare students for professional settings.

cards.we: do not allow make-up, artificial eyelashes or altered eyebrows
so: students are able to present themselves with confidence, free from pressure to conform to appearance trends.
opportunities for comparison or bullying are reduced.
a culture is fostered where students are valued for character rather than appearance.

cards.we: do not allow nail varnish or artificial nails
so: uniform expectations remain simple, consistent and equitable.
opportunities for comparison or bullying are reduced.
safety and practicality are maintained.

cards.we: do not allow students to write or draw on their skin or have visible tattoos (including temporary tattoos)
so: safeguarding is supported.
expectations remain clear and consistent for all students.
students are set up for success by removing any possibility that markings could be misinterpreted by staff or other students.

cards.we: set clear expectations for hair (off the face, tied back if hair length is below the collar, natural colour, no markings or extreme styles)
so: students are able to present themselves with confidence, free from pressure to follow trends or maintain particular styles.
opportunities for comparison, judgement or bullying based on appearance are reduced.
a culture is created where students are valued for their character, effort and conduct rather than how they look.
greater social equity is established, ensuring all students can meet expectations without disadvantage.
safeguarding is supported through clear visibility

cards.we: require no jewellery except a single pair of small plain stud earrings and an analogue watch
so: safety is maintained, particularly in practical lessons.
uniformity is upheld; variation and inequality are reduced.
students are less vulnerable to theft or unwanted attention in the community.
students are protected from inadvertently breaching JCQ examination regulations which prohibit smart watches, and the associated risks of non-compliance in public examinations.
smart watches are not used as substitutes for mobile phones (see above for why we do not allow mobile phones on site).

cards.we: only allow the academy headscarf for religious or cultural reasons, with full visibility of the face
so: inclusion and respect for identity are supported.
safeguarding and clear communication are maintained.

cards.we: use the school planner as the primary method of communication between school and home
so: parents can engage directly with their child’s day-to-day school experience, celebrating successes and responding to sanctions in a timely and informed way.
students and families can have consistent, structured conversations at home that support reflection, improvement, and positive routines.
communication remains fully inclusive and accessible to all families, regardless of access to digital devices or technology.
students are supported in developing organisation and responsibility through clear written communication they can carry with them each day.

cards.we: do not use email as a direct method of communication to individual staff from parents
so: safeguarding concerns and/or urgent issues are handled appropriately through designated channels rather than informal or fragmented communication routes.
tone, clarity, and intent are not lost or misunderstood in written exchanges, reducing the risk of miscommunication.
staff and parents/carers are protected from untimely or emotionally charged communication that may impact wellbeing or be misinterpreted without full context.
staff can focus fully on the students in their care, with individual queries addressed at an appropriate time, without disrupting learning or diverting attention from the students in front of them.

cards.we: use reception as the first point of contact for telephone communication from parents and carers
so: urgent messages are identified and directed promptly to the appropriate member of staff.
communication is handled efficiently and safely, ensuring that priority concerns are responded to in a timely manner.
staff are able to focus on teaching and student support.

cards.we: provide a dedicated non-urgent email inbox for parents and carers
so: busy families have a flexible and accessible way to communicate with the school when a phone call is not possible.
non-urgent queries are logged and responded to in an orderly and manageable way, supporting consistency and fairness of response times.
communication remains structured and does not disrupt teaching, safeguarding processes or staff workload.

cards.we: use an online platform to send attainment/progress reports, letters and whole-school communication, and expect parents/carers to regularly check the platform and acknowledge communications where required
so: families receive regular, coherent updates on progress rather than frequent or fragmented communications.
parents and carers can access and engage with information at a time that is convenient for them.
communication is consistent and standardised across the school, ensuring fairness and clarity for all families.

cards.we: expect a parent/carer or, where appropriate, an appropriate adult to attend academy meetings, including Parents’ Evenings, attendance meetings, progress or behaviour meetings and information evenings
so: parents and carers engage directly with teachers to understand their child’s progress, strengths and next steps.
strong home–school relationships are developed and maintained, supporting consistency of expectations and support.
we can ensure clear, timely and shared understanding of academic progress, behaviour and attendance priorities.

cards.we: expect students to attend school unless they are unwell, with absence reported promptly by parents/carers
so: student welfare is monitored, and safeguarding concerns can be identified quickly.
learning continuity is maintained as far as possible.

cards.we: require explanations for absence and follow up prolonged absence with communication home
so: attendance patterns are understood and supported appropriately.
students are safeguarded through consistent monitoring and communication.

cards.we: require students to catch up on missed work following absence
so: learning gaps are minimised and students remain aligned with their peers.
students take responsibility for their learning and progress.

cards.we: do not authorise holidays during term time
so: learning time is protected and not lost unnecessarily.
all students are treated fairly and consistently.

cards.we: expect all students to be on site before the gates close and to arrive punctually to all lessons
so: learning begins on time and is not disrupted.
students develop habits of punctuality and responsibility that prepare them for adult life.
staff can accurately account for all students on site, supporting safeguarding.

cards.we: require students who arrive late to report to Reception and/or their Head of Year
so: attendance is accurately recorded and monitored.
students are safely accounted for at all times.

cards.we: require students to report illness or injury immediately to a member of staff
so: students receive appropriate care and support promptly.
staff are aware of student wellbeing and can respond appropriately.

cards.we: require permission and supervision for visits to the medical room
so: students remain safe and accounted for during the school day.
medical needs are managed in a structured and controlled way.

cards.we: contact parents/carers if a student is too unwell to remain in school
so: students are supported appropriately and safely.
parents are kept informed and involved in decisions regarding wellbeing.

cards.we: require written parental consent and appropriate procedures for students taking medication in school
so: student health needs are managed safely and responsibly.
staff are not placed in a position of administering medication without proper authorisation.

cards.we: require absence requests to be submitted in writing in advance and approved by the Head of Year before students sign out at Reception and leave the site
so: students are fully accounted for at all times, supporting safeguarding.
parents/carers are aware of and authorise any absence from school during the day.
clear records are maintained of student movement on and off site.

cards.we: require attendance at after school interventions and Saturday/holiday school where students are selected or allocated
so: students receive targeted academic support to close gaps, strengthen understanding and improve outcomes.
additional teaching time is used effectively to benefit those who need it most. public resources and staffing are used responsibly, ensuring places are taken up and not wasted.
students develop commitment and responsibility towards opportunities designed to help them succeed.
students are safeguarded through clear expectations about where they should be, providing structure and reassurance for families and the school.
we support students during potentially stressful periods through structured revision and study time, reducing overwhelm and promoting wellbeing.

cards.we: provide formal written notice of compulsory sessions through school communication channels
so: parents and carers are clearly informed in advance and can support attendance.
expectations are transparent, consistent and accessible for all families.
communication remains structured and reliable.

cards.we: require students who miss sessions due to illness to provide a note from home and complete catch-up work
so: learning time is not lost and students remain supported in keeping up with their peers.
absence is managed fairly and consistently while maintaining focus on progress.

cards.we: require planned absence from sessions to be approved in advance with supporting communication and evidence, with catch-up completed
so: attendance is prioritised while recognising exceptional circumstances.
students remain accountable for completing missed learning.
communication between home and school is clear and proactive.

cards.we: apply sanctions in addition to catch up where sessions are missed without authorisation
so: students understand the importance of attending additional support put in place for their benefit.
staff time and allocated resources are respected.
expectations remain fair and consistent for all students.
students are held accountable while still being supported to complete missed learning.

cards.we: identify and assess the needs of every SEND student using a graduated (assess, plan, do, review) approach from the earliest point of concern
so: support is timely, evidence-based and responsive, rather than reactive or crisis-driven.

cards.we: actively champion each student’s strengths, nurture their resilience, and place them at the centre of every decision made about their education
so: students develop the confidence and self-belief to advocate for themselves.
families trust that their child’s best interests drive every decision.

cards.we: hold high expectations for every student with SEND, scaffolding the curriculum rather than reducing it
so: no student is limited by low expectations, and SEND is not used as a reason to narrow opportunity.

cards.we: invest in high-quality, inclusive teaching as the foundation of our universal offer
so: the needs of our weakest and most vulnerable learners are met first and foremost in the classroom, reducing dependency on additional intervention.

cards.we: train all teachers in inclusive teaching strategies so that classroom practice responds in real time to how students are learning
so: SEND students receive expert support from every teacher, every lesson, not only from specialist staff.

cards.we: maintain clear, consistent expectations and routines across every classroom and transition
so: there is no ambiguity for students who find grey areas confusing or social unpredictability difficult to navigate; the rules are the same, everywhere, always.

cards.we: build predictable structures and calm environments into the fabric of every school day
so: cognitive load is reduced for students who might otherwise spend mental energy anticipating the unknown or managing anxiety about the behaviour of those around them, freeing them to focus entirely on their learning.

cards.we: explicitly teach independence, self-regulation and life skills, as appropriate, alongside academic content
so: students develop the practical and emotional capabilities to navigate school, community, and adult life with increasing confidence.

cards.we: take a considered, individualised approach to the use of sensory tools, fidget resources, ear defenders and other adjustments, ensuring they are carefully matched to clearly identified needs, reduced over time where possible, and used in line with evidence-informed practice and professional assessment
so: students benefit from approaches that are tailored to individual student need, grounded in robust evidence and have a demonstrable impact on progress, attainment and engagement.

support is matched to the assessed need rather than the diagnostic label, ensuring that provision is built around the specific barriers to learning observed in the classroom and what evidence suggests will remove or reduce them, enabling students to access learning, make progress and achieve meaningful outcomes.

cards.we: Do not routinely use coloured overlays, tinted lenses or colour-based worksheet printing as classroom adjustments, as evidence does not show reliable improvements in reading accuracy or comprehension (Suttle, Lawrenson & Conway, 2018; Albon, Adi & Hyde, 2008; Galuschka et al., 2014), though overlays may be used temporarily where they are already established or form part of a child’s usual way of working
so: support is directed towards strategies that genuinely address the underlying difficulty, rather than interventions that may feel helpful but do not produce consistent improvements in learning.

students’ learning is supported through approaches with proven impact—such as explicit instruction, structured phonics, clear modelling and well-designed resources—rather than interventions that do not address underlying barriers or consistently improve literacy, attention or comprehension.

students are not taught to rely on surface features that do not transfer beyond the classroom, and can independently access standard printed materials they will encounter in real-world contexts (e.g. textbooks, exams, forms and everyday documents, which are not colour-adapted such as menus, timetables or official information).

we strengthen independence and self-belief, ensuring students build confidence in accessing standardised formats and are equipped for assessments, further education and adult life where materials are not modified by colour-based adaptations.
finite staff time and school resources are directed towards inclusive, adaptive teaching practices that reliably support reading, comprehension, attention and independence for students with SEND.

cards.we: provide small group classes for our most complex SEND students, when possible
so: students who are not yet ready to thrive in a full mainstream classroom environment receive the relational consistency, scaffolded learning, and specialist expertise they need to build the foundations for learning.

cards.we: track progress carefully using shared data and review evidence at regular intervals
so: movement forward is recognised and celebrated, and any regression or stagnation is identified and responded to quickly.

cards.we: favour shared teaching assistant support over assigning one adult solely to one child, even where a student needs extra adult help in the classroom
so: students build independence gradually rather than becoming reliant on one adult.
students are not inadvertently made dependent on a single adult, and instead develop the self-regulation and resilience to become as independent as possible.
students develop confidence and a sense of self that is not defined by the presence of an adult beside them.
students are encouraged to self-initiate rather than wait for adult prompts.
the class teacher remains the lead professional for the student’s learning, in line with evidence-based recommendations by the Education Endowment Fund.

cards.we: systematically reduce scaffolding as students grow in confidence and capability
so: dependency on support is not inadvertently created, and the goal of independence remains central to every student’s journey.

cards.we: ensure SEND students access the same broad, ambitious co-curricular and enrichment offer as their peers
so: every student has the opportunity to discover their strengths, build confidence and develop relationships beyond the academic curriculum.
